blocks.text: SQLite supports only one writer at a time per database file; the official guidance says short write transactions can often take turns, but client/server systems can handle substantially more write concurrency.
blocks.author: researcher-2

blocks.text: SQLite’s intended design places the database and application on the same machine; its official network guidance recommends considering client/server databases when data is on another machine, and warns that network filesystems do not support SQLite’s usual locking assumptions.
blocks.author: researcher-2

blocks.text: PostgreSQL MVCC provides statement-level snapshots and allows reads not to block writes, and writes not to block reads, in the described isolation model; locks mean it does not eliminate all contention.
blocks.author: researcher-1

blocks.text: SQLite documents flexible typing as a feature: declared column types determine affinity, and values are not constrained to a single declared type in the same way as rigidly typed engines; moving data that has relied on mixed or unexpected storage classes can require validation and cleanup before PostgreSQL constraints accept it.
blocks.author: researcher-1

blocks.text: SQLite can be used server-side when an application-specific server mediates requests and serializes database access; separate database files per user or subdomain can reduce contention, but that topology differs from one shared multi-tenant file.

comments.text: The server-mediated and per-tenant-file pattern is the main route to a SQLite-first SaaS. The brief cites only s1 for it, with no production evidence. Per-tenant files turn cross-tenant queries, schema migrations across N files, backups of N files and connection management into application work. A five-person team may find that burden larger than managed Postgres. Single-machine placement also means a host failure causes downtime or data loss unless a replication or proxy layer exists, which s5 only mentions. The brief understates these costs.

comments.text: The 100,000 hits/day figure comes from the SQLite project's own page. It is a conservative traffic estimate, not a measure of write load. A SaaS with authenticated users, background jobs and many writes per request can hit the single-writer limit (b1) at far lower traffic. s2 describes lock starvation of unlucky writers. Using this figure as support for SQLite as a SaaS default is vendor-sourced and mismatched to the workload. The brief should state a write-rate threshold instead.

comments.text: The server-mediated and per-tenant-file pattern is the main route to a SQLite-first SaaS. The brief cites only s1 for it, with no production evidence. Per-tenant files turn cross-tenant queries, schema migrations across N files, backups of N files and connection management into application work. A five-person team may find that burden larger than managed Postgres. Single-machine placement also means a host failure causes downtime or data loss unless a replication or proxy layer exists, which s5 only mentions. The brief understates these costs.

blocks.text: SQLite may avoid unnecessary infrastructure for a small single-node application. This changes the recommendation when local access, low contention, and acceptable recovery are deliberate constraints—not merely assumptions about an early-stage product.

blocks.text: Serialized app-server, per-tenant-file, and proxy designs can make SQLite a viable SaaS architecture. Their strongest objection to the default is real, but the supplied material lacks production comparisons of their operational burden; evaluate cross-tenant reporting, fleet-wide migrations, and backups before choosing them.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: The reliability comparison is asymmetric: managed RDS features are not an equal-RPO/RTO comparison with a fully operated SQLite platform. This lowers confidence in a general reliability winner, but does not overturn the Postgres default for a conventional shared-database deployment.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Managed Postgres is neither maintenance-free nor necessarily inexpensive. The team still must select and verify a suitable tier, monitor workload behavior, and test recovery; a cheap entry plan is not evidence of production HA.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor wrote Risks

blocks.text: SQLite growth risk: longer transactions or overlapping writers can increase lock waits. Test representative request traffic and background jobs together; no defensible universal writes-per-second threshold is available here.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: SQLite recovery risk: replication and restore commands do not establish health detection, replacement-host provisioning, promotion, or traffic switching. Assign ownership and rehearse those steps rather than assuming Litestream provides automatic failover.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Migration risk is conditional and unquantified. SQLite’s documented flexible typing suggests that applications relying on mixed-type values may need validation or cleanup when moving to stricter typing; this is an inference, not evidence that every SQLite migration is costly.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Postgres purchasing risk: a plan may lack the required HA or recovery coverage, while contention remains possible despite MVCC. Verify the actual service configuration rather than buying on an entry price or an engine-level promise.

decisions: Use three working agents: one researcher per database and one skeptic; the automatically added Editor and Gap Detector keep the total, including the Orchestrator, at six agents.
